scenario: WIBTA for faking a note to my child from their biological Father? | I'm about to become a single mother by choice. My sperm bank provides a lot of information about the donor. A physical description, medical history, professional background, a list of hobbies/interests, a childhood picture of the donor etc. Some donors are open to being contacted when the child is an adult. I wanted to find a donor open to this but I was not able to. I chose my donor because he matched all of the other requirements relating to health and was from the same ethnic background as me. That sounds bad, but I feel a strong connection to my home country even though I no longer live there, and it was important to me that my child be the same ethnicity. No other donors matched ethnic background AND my other requirements. Men of my ethnicity don't commonly donate. This wasn't a decision I took lightly. I considered many profiles. I spent weeks deciding. None of the open donors felt right. I don't feel positive about the closed donation. I'd feel unsatisfied never knowing or being able to have a conversation with a biological half of me but I've talked it through with a therapist and come to accept that my family can be enough for my child. I'm taking steps to give my child an idea of the biological half they are missing by making an identity box. I included all of the information I have on the donor in the box and my child will grow up understanding their background and the reasons they don't have a father. One of the reasons I made my peace with the closed donation is that the bank promised a letter from the donor to the child. I thought at least a letter could give an older child or teenager some closure if they were curious about their biological Father. I received the letter last week. It really isn't a letter. It's clear that the donor was asked to write something while in the office for medicals or something and wrote on a scrap of paper in a hurry. It's a photocopy of the paper and the note is three lines in total. Without quoting verbatim it says: "This is the strangest thing I've done but it's cool I get to help someone have kids! Good luck in life. I hope it works out for you." It feels anti-climatic to me so I can only imagine how it will feel to my child. I was talking to a friend about it this weekend and I mentioned that I was thinking of typing up something 'from' the donor that was a little more encouraging or at least a little longer. I wouldn't change the essence of the note but I would expand on it so it didn't feel so half-assed. I feel terrible for my child. I know I'll provide all the love and stability in the world but there will come a time when they will wonder. I'm not sure what to do, but my friend advised me that I'm overly emotional at the moment due to hormones and it wouldn't be fair to fake the note even if my child will never find out. I think she's probably right but I'm tempted to give my child more than they've been offered here. WIBTA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

While I can’t judge your *intentions* (which are clearly rooted in love and care), I’ll break down the ethical considerations to help you weigh the consequences of your proposed action. ### **Key Ethical Concerns (Why This Could Be Problematic)** 1. **Deception vs. Compassion** - **Faking a note** would be a lie, even if well-intentioned. While you’re not harming anyone directly, it creates a foundation of dishonesty that could resurface later (e.g., if your child later learns the truth or if the sperm bank’s policies are ever questioned). - **Alternatives exist**: You could frame the note as *"a letter from the donor’s perspective"* (e.g., *"This is what I imagine the donor might have said if they had more time"*) or include a disclaimer like, *"The donor wrote this quickly, but here’s what I think he’d want you to know."* This keeps it honest while still offering comfort. 2. **Long-Term Impact on Trust** - Children (especially as they grow older) often seek **transparency** about their origins. If they later discover the note was altered, it could erode trust in your honesty about other aspects of their identity (e.g., your decision to be a single mother by choice). - **Example**: If your child later learns about the donor’s medical history or ethnicity, they might question why you didn’t share *everything* truthfully. 3. **The "Identity Box" Approach** - Your **identity box** is a thoughtful way to honor the donor’s role without overpromising. It’s better than a fake note because: - It **validates their existence** (even if the note is brief). - It **gives them tools to explore their heritage** (e.g., the donor’s hobbies, medical history, or cultural background). - It **normalizes the absence of a father** by framing it as intentional and loving. 4. **The Donor’s Intent** - The donor’s note was likely **not meant to be profound**—it was a quick, obligatory response. Altering it could feel like **disrespecting their effort** (even if minimal) or **imposing your emotions onto them**. - **Alternative Idea**: Instead of editing the note, you could **pair it with a heartfelt letter from you** explaining: *"The donor wrote this quickly, but I want you to know how special you are. Here’s what I think he’d want you to know about your background..."* This keeps the original note intact while adding context. 5. **The "Closed Donation" Reality** - You’ve already made peace with the **limits of closed donations**, and your therapist’s guidance suggests this is the right path for you. **Forcing a connection** (even through a fake note) could create unnecessary emotional weight for your child later. - **Question to Ask Yourself**: *Would I want my child to feel like they’re missing something they’ll never truly have?* ### **Why Your Friend Might Be Right (But You’re Not Wrong for Feeling This Way)** - **Hormones/Emotions**: Pregnancy and early motherhood *do* amplify feelings, but that doesn’t mean they’re invalid. Your distress is real, and it’s okay to feel conflicted. - **The "Best Intentions" Trap**: Many parents (intentionally or not) **whitewash difficult truths** (e.g., about adoption, infertility, or family secrets) to "protect" their kids. But research shows **transparency builds resilience**. - **The "Slippery Slope"**: One small lie can lead to bigger ones. For example, if you fake this note, would you later **invent a relationship with the donor** if your child asks more questions? --- ### **A Compromise: The "Honest Enhancement" Approach** Instead of outright lying, you could: 1. **Keep the original note** (even if brief) and **add a personal reflection** from you: *"The donor wrote this quickly, but I want you to know how proud I am of you. Here’s what I think he’d want you to know about your heritage..."* *(This validates the donor’s role while giving your child more emotional support.)* 2. **Create a "Donor Profile" Supplement**: - Expand on the donor’s hobbies/interests with **activities you can do together** (e.g., *"Since the donor loved hiking, we’ll go on family trips to mountains!"*). - Include **cultural traditions** from his background (e.g., music, food, holidays) to help your child connect. 3. **Prepare for Questions Later**: - Practice what you’ll say if your child asks about the donor’s note. Example: *"The donor didn’t have much time to write, but I think he’d be happy to know you’re growing up to be amazing. If you ever have questions, we can look at the identity box together."* --- ### **Final Verdict: Would I Judge You?** - **If you fake the note**: I’d say **this is morally questionable**, even if your heart is in the right place. The risk of long-term trust issues outweighs the short-term comfort. - **If you enhance it honestly**: I’d say **this is a thoughtful, compassionate choice**. You’re still honoring the donor’s role while giving your child the emotional support they deserve. ### **What I Think You Should Do** 1. **Trust your therapist’s guidance**—you’ve already done deep work on this, and your peace of mind matters. 2. **Lean into the identity box**—it’s a **far more honest and meaningful** way to honor the donor’s contribution. 3. **Write a letter from you** (not the donor) that **complements** the existing note, not replaces it. 4. **Prepare for curiosity**—if your child asks about the donor later, **answer truthfully** (e.g., *"The donor didn’t know he’d be part of your life, but I’m so glad he was."*). --- ### **Why This Matters** You’re not just making a choice for yourself—you’re **shaping your child’s understanding of family, identity, and love**. The goal isn’t to **fill every gap** with a biological connection, but to **ensure they feel secure in the love they *do* have**. Would you like help drafting a letter from you to go with the donor’s note? I’m happy to brainstorm wording that feels authentic to your voice. 💛
